connection: This opening session establishes the feedback loop every later lesson relies on: find the project, make one change, build it, run it, and verify the result.
objectives: Explain the different jobs performed by a solution and a project file.
Trace source code through build output to observable application behavior.
Use restore, build, run, and test as separate feedback steps.
Interpret a successful command as evidence, not as proof of every possible behavior.

visuals.title: A solution organizes projects
visuals.explanation: TimeClock.sln groups the application, domain library, and test project. Each project still owns its target framework, references, and build output.

visuals.title: Source becomes runnable output
visuals.explanation: The compiler checks C# source and produces assemblies. A successful build means compilation succeeded; running the app is a separate observation.

visuals.title: Short loops expose mistakes early
visuals.explanation: Edit one thing, build, observe the result, and adjust. Small loops make cause and effect easier to identify than a large batch of changes.

visuals.title: Tests check stated behavior
visuals.explanation: Tests supply inputs and compare actual behavior with expectations. They complement the build because compiling successfully does not prove a business rule.

preQuiz.prompt: If TimeClock.sln is removed but the three project files remain, what is most directly lost?
options: The grouping used to build and test the projects together
preQuiz.explanation: Projects still contain source and build configuration, but the solution-level grouping is gone.

preQuiz.prompt: A Release build succeeds. What can you safely conclude?
options: The included projects compiled without build errors
preQuiz.explanation: Build success proves compilation, not every runtime path or business expectation.

preQuiz.prompt: Why run tests after a successful build?
options: Tests check selected behavior the compiler cannot judge
preQuiz.explanation: The compiler checks language and type rules; tests check examples of intended behavior.

concept.title: Solution versus project
paragraphs: A solution is an organizing boundary. It lets one command address several related projects. A project is a build boundary: it declares its target framework, references, and output type.
TimeClock.App is executable, TimeClock.Domain is a reusable library, and TimeClock.Domain.Tests is a test project. Their names communicate responsibility before you open a source file.

concept.title: Four commands, four questions
paragraphs: Restore asks whether required packages can be resolved. Build asks whether source compiles. Run asks what the executable does. Test asks whether selected behavior matches explicit expectations.
Keeping those questions separate makes failures easier to locate. A restore failure is not diagnosed like a failing assertion, and a compiler error is not investigated like surprising console output.
concept.code:
dotnet restore TimeClock.sln
dotnet build TimeClock.sln --configuration Release
dotnet run --project src/TimeClock.App/TimeClock.App.csproj
dotnet test TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

concept.title: Read output as evidence
paragraphs: A zero exit code and a clean build are concrete signals. They are deliberately narrower than 'the application is correct.' Good engineering names what was checked and what remains unobserved.
This course records validation commands in the manifest so lesson claims stay tied to repeatable evidence.

lab.objective: Change one observable application label and prove that the edited project is the one being executed.
lab.startingCondition: The solution builds, seven domain tests pass, and the console begins with TimeClock sample.
steps: Open src/TimeClock.App/Program.cs and predict which output line will change.
Change the first heading to TimeClock course application.
Build TimeClock.sln in Release configuration and distinguish build output from application output.
Run TimeClock.App and confirm only the predicted heading changed.
Run the full test suite and confirm the domain tests still pass.
lab.expectedBehavior: The first line is TimeClock course application; worker and duration output remain unchanged; all tests pass.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet run --project src/TimeClock.App/TimeClock.App.csproj --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Publish the synchronized lesson, lab, and quizzes.

commit: session-01: teach the dotnet solution feedback loop
review: The application change is limited to the intended output label.
The documented commands use repository-relative paths.
The Release build completes without warnings or errors.
The console output matches the documented expectation.

postQuiz.prompt: The heading changes after dotnet run, while tests remain green. What does that combination show?
options: The app project changed and the tested domain behavior remained intact
The solution file contains the heading
postQuiz.explanation: The run observes the app change; the tests independently protect selected domain behavior.

postQuiz.prompt: What would most likely happen if the App project reference to Domain were removed?
options: Program.cs could no longer resolve ClockEntry
xUnit would become part of the app
postQuiz.explanation: TimeClock.App uses ClockEntry from the referenced domain assembly.

postQuiz.prompt: Why keep the lab change small?
options: It isolates the likely cause of the observed output change
It prevents the compiler from running
postQuiz.explanation: A small change makes the connection between edit and behavior easier to reason about.

reflections: Which command gave evidence about compilation, and which gave evidence about behavior?
How would you tell whether a failure belongs to restore, build, run, or test?
What does a successful test run still not prove?
whatBreaks: Removing the solution loses the convenient all-project build and test boundary. Removing the App-to-Domain project reference breaks compilation because Program.cs uses ClockEntry. Removing the output line does not affect domain rules, but it removes the visible signal the lab intentionally changed.
summary: A .NET solution organizes projects; each project defines a build boundary. Restore, build, run, and test answer different questions, and a short feedback loop turns their output into specific evidence.
